The Federal Government has vowed to intensify enforcement against counterfeit, adulterated and substandard seeds, warning that their circulation threatens agricultural productivity, farmers’ livelihoods and efforts to achieve food security in Nigeria. The government also unveiled the National Seed Sector Roadmap for 2026–2031 to attract investments, strengthen regulatory oversight and improve farmers’ access to quality planting materials. The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Abubakar Kyari, disclosed this at the ninth SeedConnect Africa Conference and Exhibition in Abuja on Tuesday. According to a statement issued by the ministry’s Head of Information, Ezeaja Ikemefuna, the minister, represented by the Permanent Secretary, Marcus Ogunbiyi, called for stronger regulatory enforcement alongside efforts to expand regional seed trade. The statement read, “Kyari said that harmonised regulatory standards, improved certification systems, and effective cross-border cooperation can facilitate the movement of quality seeds across national boundaries, expand markets for domestic enterprises, and improve farmers’ access to suitable varieties. “He stressed, however, that such integration cannot succeed while counterfeit, adulterated, and poor-quality seeds continue to threaten agricultural productivity, adding that the Federal Government will keep strengthening the National Agricultural Seeds Council to handle seed certification, quality assurance, market surveillance, and standards enforcement.” Kyari advocated the adoption of digital traceability, electronic verification and reliable seed identification systems to enable farmers to verify the authenticity of planting materials and help regulators monitor compliance. He explained that investments in fertiliser, irrigation, mechanisation and agricultural extension services would not achieve their full potential without access to quality seeds. The minister said the government would encourage the development, multiplication and commercialisation of improved seed varieties capable of withstanding drought, heat, flooding, pests and diseases. He also advocated the production of nutrient-rich crops to improve nutrition, urging research institutions to strengthen collaboration with seed companies, agricultural processors and farmers. On financing, Kyari identified limited access to affordable credit as a major constraint facing Africa’s seed industry, particularly small and medium enterprises. He urged commercial banks, development finance institutions, insurance companies and private investors to explore blended financing, credit guarantees, agricultural insurance and risk-sharing arrangements. Its responsibility is to create an enabling environment, strengthen institutions, reduce investment risks and mobilise private capital,” the statement noted. Kyari further called for harmonised regulatory standards, improved certification systems and cross-border cooperation to expand market opportunities for Nigerian seed producers across Africa. He reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to implementing the outcomes of the African Union’s inaugural continental Seed Summit, held in Eswatini between October 5 and 7, 2026, subject to formal endorsement by African leaders and alignment with national priorities. The minister also cited the Plant Variety Protection Act, 2021, and Nigeria’s accession to the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants in March 2025 as measures to protect breeders’ rights and encourage investment in crop improvement. He stressed the need to strengthen seed distribution networks, expand access to agro-dealer outlets and improve the availability of planting materials for crops such as cassava, yam and cocoa. Kyari directed the council to collaborate with relevant institutions and private sector stakeholders to develop an implementation framework for the conference’s recommendations, with clearly defined responsibilities, timelines and measurable targets. Earlier, the Director-General of the National Agricultural Seeds Council, Fatuhu Muhammed, identified inadequate financing, infrastructure gaps, limited adoption of improved varieties and weak linkages between research and commercial seed production as persistent challenges facing the industry. Muhammed described the newly unveiled five-year roadmap as a framework for coordinating investments and interventions towards building a productive, resilient and commercially viable seed industry. He encouraged seed companies to leverage the conference to establish partnerships, attract investments and strengthen business relationships. The PUNCH reported in September 2025 that the NASC pledged tougher measures to eliminate fake seeds from circulation and ensure Nigeria’s agricultural produce meets global export standards. In 2019, the council introduced SeedCodex, an electronic authentication technology that allows farmers to verify the authenticity of seeds through unique identification codes sent via text messages. The National Agricultural Seeds Council Act, 2019, also criminalises unlicensed commercial seed production and marketing, misleading labelling and fraudulent practices in the sale of seeds.
